items.question: A transaction runs the same query twice and gets different rows each time, even though it has not committed. Which phenomenon is this?
items.explanation: Page 2 defines a non-repeatable read as the same query returning different rows within one transaction; a dirty read involves reading uncommitted changes.

items.question: Why would a database designer choose a weaker isolation level rather than the strongest one?
options: A. Weaker isolation provides more durability
B. Stronger isolation levels allow less concurrency, so weaker ones permit more simultaneous work
C. Weaker isolation eliminates the write-ahead log
D. Weaker isolation makes transactions atomic
items.explanation: Page 2 states stronger isolation levels prevent more anomalies but allow less concurrency, so there is a trade-off.

items.question: What does SERIALIZABLE isolation guarantee about the outcome of concurrent transactions?
items.correct_answer: It gives a result equal to some serial order of the transactions, as if they had run one after another.
items.explanation: Page 2 defines SERIALIZABLE as producing the result of some serial order of the transactions.

items.question: Explain how the write-ahead log ensures that a committed transaction's changes survive a crash.
items.correct_answer: The log record is flushed to disk before COMMIT returns, so after a crash the log can be replayed to redo the committed work.
items.explanation: Page 3 states the log is written before commit returns and replayed after a crash to redo committed work.

items.question: A bank transfer debits account A and credits account B. A crash occurs after the debit is applied but before the credit. Which ACID-related mechanism ensures the debit is undone?
options: A. Isolation, because the partial transaction is invisible
B. Durability, because the log is replayed
C. Atomicity, because a failure rolls back every statement in the transaction
D. Consistency, because constraints are checked
items.explanation: Page 1 defines atomicity as all-or-nothing: a failure rolls back every statement, and page 3 uses this transfer as the example of the debit never happening without the credit.
